topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Relations and functions
topic.scope: Input-output machines; ordered pairs; domain, co-domain and range; one input giving exactly one output; vertical line test; function notation f(x) is not f times x; evaluating f(a+b) is not f(a)+f(b).

nodes.name: Relation is any subset of pairs
A machine gives output by a fixed rule
Every input has exactly one output
Different inputs may share an output
Every domain element must be used
Vertical line cuts graph at most once
f(x) is a name for the output, not f times x
external_prereqs: multiplication shown by writing side by side

nodes.name: Replace x by the whole input in brackets
Domain is the set of allowed inputs
Range is a subset of co-domain

misconceptions.statement: The pair (2, 5) and the pair (5, 2) are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Students treat pairs like sets, where order does not matter.
misconceptions.fix: In an ordered pair the first number is the input or x-value and the second is the output or y-value, so (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different pairs.

probe.question: Is the point (3, 4) the same as the point (4, 3)?

misconceptions.root_belief: order of items does not change meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' understanding of coordinates and ordered pairs

misconceptions.statement: A relation must follow a neat formula connecting the numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students mostly meet relations as formulas like y = 2x.
misconceptions.fix: A relation is any collection of ordered pairs from two sets; a rule or formula is not required.

probe.question: Is {(1, 5), (2, 9), (3, 1)} a relation from A = {1,2,3} to B = {1,5,9}?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is no rule joining the numbers.

misconceptions.root_belief: every connection must follow a visible pattern

misconceptions.statement: A relation must include every possible pair of the two sets.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse a relation with the full Cartesian product.
misconceptions.fix: A relation is only some chosen pairs, a subset of the Cartesian product A × B.

probe.question: A = {1,2}, B = {3,4}. Is {(1,3)} a relation from A to B?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must have all four pairs.

misconceptions.root_belief: a part is treated as the whole

misconceptions.statement: A function machine must always do arithmetic on the input.
misconceptions.why: Textbook machines are usually 'add 3' or 'multiply by 2'.
misconceptions.fix: A rule can be any definite assignment, such as 'give the day after', a table, or a list of pairs.

probe.question: A machine gives each student's roll number the student's class. Is it a function machine?

misconceptions.root_belief: the textbook example is the only kind

misconceptions.statement: A function can give two different outputs for the same input.
misconceptions.why: Students think any rule linking two quantities counts as a function.
misconceptions.fix: In a function each input gives exactly one output; one input with two outputs is not a function.

probe.question: Is {(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)} a function?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every pair is a valid link.

misconceptions.root_belief: any connection counts as a function
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' concept image of function (e.g. Vinner and Dreyfus type studies)

misconceptions.statement: If a rule is a function in one direction, its reverse is also a function.
misconceptions.why: Students think connections work equally both ways.
misconceptions.fix: A function need not be reversible; the reverse pairs may give one input two outputs.

probe.question: f = {(1,5),(2,5)}. Reversed, is {(5,1),(5,2)} a function?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since f was a function.

misconceptions.root_belief: relationships are symmetric

misconceptions.statement: Two different inputs cannot give the same output in a function.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up 'one output per input' with 'one input per output'.
misconceptions.fix: Only one input giving two outputs is forbidden; many inputs may share the same output, as in f(x) = x².
misconceptions.root_belief: repeating a value is always an error
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties with the univalence condition of functions

misconceptions.statement: A rule is still a function if some elements of the domain have no output.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the pairs that appear and ignore missing elements.
misconceptions.fix: Every element of the domain must be assigned an output for the rule to be a function on that domain.

probe.question: Domain {1,2,3}; pairs {(1,2),(2,4)}. Is this a function from the domain?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, no input has two outputs.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is not shown does not matter

misconceptions.statement: A graph is a function if no horizontal line cuts it twice.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the vertical test with the horizontal one used for one-one functions.
misconceptions.fix: The vertical line test checks functions: a vertical line cutting a graph twice means one x has two y-values, so it is not a function.

probe.question: The parabola y = x² is cut twice by the line y = 4. Does that make it a non-function?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is not a function.

misconceptions.root_belief: a test works in any direction
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student graph interpretation of functions

misconceptions.statement: Only a straight line or smooth curve can be the graph of a function.
misconceptions.why: Students see mostly lines and parabolas.
misconceptions.fix: Any graph passing the vertical line test is a function, even a set of separate dots or a stepped graph.

probe.question: Three separate dots with different x-values: is it a function graph?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are not joined in a line.

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture is the only valid one
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototypes in students' concept images of function

misconceptions.statement: A circle is the graph of a function because it is a smooth curve.
misconceptions.why: Students judge by smoothness and regular shape, not by the test.
misconceptions.fix: A vertical line cuts a circle at two points, so one x-value has two y-values and it is not a function.

probe.question: Is the circle x² + y² = 25 the graph of a function?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a smooth regular curve.

misconceptions.root_belief: neat looking shapes follow the rules

misconceptions.statement: In f(x), the f and x are multiplied together.
misconceptions.why: In algebra, letters written side by side mean multiplication, as in ab.
misconceptions.fix: f(x) is read 'f of x' and means the output the function f gives for input x; it is not f times x.

probe.question: If f(x) = 3x + 1, what is f(2)?

misconceptions.root_belief: side by side letters always mean multiplication
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' misreading of function notation as multiplication

misconceptions.statement: f(x) can be simplified by cancelling x, as f(x)/x = f.
misconceptions.why: Students treat f as a number that multiplies x.
misconceptions.fix: f(x) is one output value; you cannot cancel x from it. Dividing it by x gives a new expression to work out.

probe.question: If f(x) = x + 5, simplify f(x)/x.

misconceptions.root_belief: letters in algebra can always be cancelled

misconceptions.statement: f(a + b) equals f(a) + f(b) for every function.
misconceptions.why: Students treat f like multiplication, which distributes over addition.
misconceptions.fix: This holds only for special rules like f(x) = 2x; for f(x) = x² it fails, so each value must be calculated directly.

probe.question: f(x) = x². Find f(2 + 3).

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on overgeneralised linearity in school algebra

misconceptions.statement: f(2x) is always the same as 2 times f(x).
misconceptions.why: Students apply the pattern of pulling out a multiplier.
misconceptions.fix: f(2x) means putting 2x in as the input, which usually differs from 2f(x); for f(x) = x + 1, f(2x) = 2x + 1 but 2f(x) = 2x + 2.

probe.question: f(x) = x + 1. Find f(2x).

misconceptions.root_belief: operations always pull out of brackets
misconceptions.source_hint: research on linearity illusion in student reasoning

misconceptions.statement: For f(x) = x², f(-3) is -9.
misconceptions.why: Students square only the number and keep the minus sign outside.
misconceptions.fix: Replace x by (-3) in brackets: f(-3) = (-3)² = 9.

probe.question: If f(x) = x², find f(-3).

misconceptions.root_belief: signs stay outside and are not part of the number
misconceptions.source_hint: research on errors substituting negative numbers into expressions

misconceptions.why: Students add the new part at the end rather than replacing x.
misconceptions.fix: Replace every x with (x + 1): f(x + 1) = 2(x + 1) + 3 = 2x + 5.

probe.question: f(x) = 2x + 3. Find f(x + 1).

misconceptions.root_belief: changes are added on at the end

misconceptions.statement: In f(3), the number 3 is the output of the function.
misconceptions.why: Students see the number in brackets as the answer shown.
misconceptions.fix: The number inside the brackets is the input; the output is the value of f(3) after the rule is used.

probe.question: For f(x) = x + 4, what is the output of f(3)?

misconceptions.root_belief: the first number seen is the answer

misconceptions.statement: The domain of every function is all real numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students mostly meet polynomial examples with no restrictions.
misconceptions.fix: The domain is the set of allowed inputs; some rules, such as 1/x, cannot accept every number, and a domain may be given as a smaller set.

probe.question: What number cannot be put into f(x) = 1/(x − 2)?
probe.wrong_answer: None, any number can go in.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from familiar cases works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The domain is the set of outputs of the function.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the terms domain and range.
misconceptions.fix: The domain is the set of inputs; the outputs form the range.

probe.question: For {(1,3),(2,5)}, what is the domain?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students confusing domain and range

misconceptions.statement: The range and the co-domain are always the same set.
misconceptions.why: Both are described as sets of outputs.
misconceptions.fix: The co-domain is the set where outputs are allowed to lie; the range is the part of it actually reached.

probe.question: f: {1,2} → {1,2,3,4}, f(x) = x. What is the range?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulty distinguishing co-domain and range

misconceptions.statement: The range of f(x) = x² includes negative numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students think any real number can be an output.
misconceptions.fix: A square is never negative, so the range of f(x) = x² on real numbers is only values 0 or greater.

probe.question: Can -4 be in the range of f(x) = x² on real numbers?

misconceptions.root_belief: outputs have no restrictions

misconceptions.statement: The range lists each output as many times as it occurs.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the second numbers of the pairs including repeats.
misconceptions.fix: The range is a set, so each different output is written only once.

probe.question: For {(1,4),(2,4),(3,9)}, what is the range?

misconceptions.root_belief: copy everything seen without thinking about sets

misconceptions.statement: An input-output machine works only with numbers as inputs.
misconceptions.why: School machine examples use only numbers.
misconceptions.fix: Inputs and outputs can be any objects, such as names, shapes or days, as long as a rule is definite.

probe.question: Machine: input a student's name, output the student's age. Can this be a function machine?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the input is not a number.

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual example is the only kind
